You’d see some guy with a table, hawking everything from old car parts to rusty kitchenware and, of course, knock-off sunglasses. Looking back on it, it wasn't so much about the value of the items but the sheer gall of it all. The ‘mark’ would have every right to be offended and yet, no one ever gave a damn.

What are the wrong depictions of the US in Hollywood movies? I've always found it fascinating how Hollywood, with its penchant for grand narratives, often paints America with broad strokes, sometimes veering far from reality. One consistent misrepresentation, in my opinion, is the portrayal of American exceptionalism. Movies often present the US as the unwavering beacon of hope, always saving the day, irrespective of the context or the complexities of the situation. While I understand the appeal of a heroic narrative, this depiction frequently glosses over the nuances of US foreign policy, historical actions, and internal struggles. It’s almost as if the scriptwriters are afraid to show any blemishes or contradictions, presenting a sanitized version of the country.Another common trope is the oversaturation of wealth and affluence. The sprawling mansions, luxury cars, and seemingly endless disposable income often depicted, while aspirational, does not reflect the lived experience of a significant portion of the American population. The focus on the upper echelons of society ignores the struggles of the working class and the widening gap between the rich and the poor that is apparent in a modern-day US. There is little acknowledgement of the cost of this 'American Dream' and the sacrifices that go into appearing as such.Furthermore, Hollywood often simplifies American culture into easily digestible stereotypes. The all-American cheerleader, the gruff but lovable law enforcer, and the eccentric tech genius are all familiar archetypes that often overshadow the diverse tapestry of American society. The complexities of cultural clashes, regional differences, and the multi-ethnic makeup of the country are frequently downplayed in favor of these readily available stereotypes. It's like an artist using only a few basic colors to paint a picture of a vibrant, multifaceted landscape. It might be visually appealing, but it's definitely incomplete.

What movie felt like you were right there with the actors? I’d have to say *Children of Men*. What other film begins with the line, "My name is Theo Faron," and later proceeds to have the protagonist experience, so vividly, the chaos of London? The film immerses you from the outset. I’m not necessarily a fan of the shaky-cam, cinematic technique, but director Alfonso Cuarón uses it with expert precision. It complements the overall narrative and gives the film an undeniable, documentary-like feel. The grittiness of the cinematography, the dimly lit scenes, and the ever-present sense of dread create an atmosphere that is both enthralling and unsettling. You witness the world through Theo's eyes, experiencing the pandemonium, the desperation, and the unrelenting uncertainty of a world on the brink of collapse.The film's action is depicted in long, continuous takes, which heightens the sense of immediacy and puts you right in the middle of the action. The harrowing bus ambush, the desperate escape from the burning refugee camp, the tense confrontation in the maternity ward; all of these scenes are masterfully crafted to pull you deeper into the narrative. The viewer becomes a bystander, privy to the characters’ most intimate moments, shared only between them and you the viewer.There's a palpable sense of realism in *Children of Men* that makes it unlike other films. The world feels lived-in, the characters feel authentic, and the events feel disturbingly plausible. The film's success lies in its ability to create a sensory experience. It goes beyond simply telling a story; it makes you *feel* it. It’s a movie that makes you breathe in the same air, see the same sights, and experience the same terrors. It's a film that is not only seen but *felt*. It’s a cinematic experience you can’t only just watch; it is one you have to live.

What are some dirty tactics used by fast food restaurants? Fast food chains are notorious for their marketing strategies, some of which tread the line into morally questionable territory. One tactic that stands out is the manipulation of portion sizes and pricing. You'll often find that the "value" meals are cleverly designed to encourage overconsumption. A small soda, for instance, might seem like a deal, but the upsize to a medium or large is often only a few cents more, subtly pushing you towards more sugar and calories. The focus isn't on providing a genuine deal, but on maximizing profit margins by selling larger quantities. Then there is the ever-present psychological manipulation.They employ things like limited-time offers (LTOs), which create a sense of urgency. Suddenly, you *need* that special burger or dessert before it disappears, even if you weren't initially hungry. They craft enticing commercials that focus on close-up shots of food, lighting, music, and voiceovers designed to make you salivate. These advertisements are engineered to bypass rational thought and trigger an impulse to buy. But perhaps the most insidious tactic of all is the use of highly processed ingredients. These are designed to be hyper-palatable, overloading your taste buds with salt, sugar, and fat, making it difficult to stop eating. It’s a cycle of craving, consumption, and, ultimately, disappointment. And they get away with it every single day. You can't blame them, but the consumer has to be aware and on guard at all times.

How would you handle an employee who refuses to attend company parties? Well, it depends, doesn’t it? In the real world, you get all sorts of folks. Those who love to party, those who are indifferent, and those who downright despise the notion of a company-sponsored get-together. I am well within my own self assigned remit to address this from a strictly practical viewpoint given my academic background in management, without getting too bogged down in the human stuff. The first question I would ask is, what are company parties meant to achieve? What is the aim? If it is to foster team camaraderie or boost morale, then, yes, there's a valid concern. If it is just a yearly formality, then I'd say leave the individual alone. Secondly, and this is critical, what does the employee's job description require? Are they a team leader, for instance? Do they need to have strong interpersonal skills? Are they working in a role that requires them to socialize with clients and vendors? If yes, then maybe it is important for them to at least make an appearance at these parties. It can be argued that these parties are very important to their jobs and as such, the party is a work requirement. However, there is no such thing as free time in the modern work environment. I would however be very mindful to ensure that the parties are not just a way for the company to get free labour. If it is, then it isn't so important that this individual doesn't show up. Let’s be frank. Not everyone thrives in social situations, and forcing someone into an environment where they are uncomfortable is a sure-fire way to make them disgruntled and, possibly, unproductive. I've met many, many people from all walks of life and the ones that are most successful are the ones that play to their strengths. If they can be a star while keeping themselves separate from the revelry, let them be. Finally, is it due to a cultural or religious reason? You can’t exclude these in the modern workplace. Some people's faith or traditions prevent them from participation in certain activities or settings. In Trinidad, we have a very diverse cultural mix. To expect an employee to go against his or her religious and cultural customs is going to be a source of conflict. As for the employee, if they are so opposed to the idea that they don't wish to attend at all, then a simple compromise is in order. Communicate, communicate, communicate. The best solution is usually a conversation; there is never a one-size-fits-all answer.

What is your biggest and weirdest pet peeve ever? I am generally a laid-back person, but there are certain things that trigger a visceral reaction within me. Some things are simply irksome, while others are downright annoying. I've come to realize that my biggest and weirdest pet peeve is the ubiquitous and often misguided use of the term "literally". It's not just the occasional misuse, but the pervasive, almost manic, incorporation of "literally" into everyday speech, often in contexts where its intended meaning of "in the exact sense of the word" is clearly and utterly nonsensical. I find myself mentally cringing when I hear someone say something like, "I was literally dying of laughter" or "My head is literally going to explode." It's as if people believe that adding "literally" to a sentence somehow amplifies its rhetorical impact, when, in reality, it often does the opposite, creating a comedic effect. It's a verbal tic, a linguistic crutch, and a signifier of a general disregard for the precision and nuance of language. I observe this usage across a varied set of environments, whether it be on social media, in media portrayals, or in personal conversations with associates. Its popularity has increased significantly as well recently.

What movies were so bad they actually made you angry, frustrated, or even caused you to walk out before the end? I’ve been on both sides of the fence when it comes to movies. I’ve sat through some downright dreadful films that made me question my life choices, and I've also had my fair share of unexpectedly pleasant cinematic experiences. However, there's a specific type of cinematic abomination that stirs a unique blend of ire and bewilderment within me: the movie that insults not just my intelligence, but also the very art of filmmaking.One such offender was a certain superhero film, which I won't name to spare it further public scorn. The trailers promised a grand, sweeping adventure, a tale of heroic deeds and epic battles. What I got was a convoluted plot, paper-thin characters, and dialogue so stale that I thought my popcorn might actually start to rot. The special effects, which should have been a highlight, were instead a garish, over-the-top display that felt more like a video game than a cinematic spectacle. The worst part? The movie seemed to revel in its own mediocrity. It was as if the filmmakers were daring me to walk out, confident that the name recognition alone would keep audiences glued to their seats.I lasted about an hour before making my exit. I remember feeling a potent mix of anger and disappointment. I felt cheated out of my time, and I couldn't help but wonder how such a project could even get the green light. The sad thing is, it garnered a lot of money at the box office, proving that I'm probably in the minority on this matter. But perhaps this is why I appreciate films like the "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" so much.

What are some plot holes in some of famous movies? Recently rewatched the 2009 Star Trek film. Don't get me wrong I absolutely love this movie. I think by a long shot it is the greatest reimagining of a popular series and one of the greatest sci-fi adventures of the 21st century. However this part of the plot sticks out like a sore thumb for me. Nero, an angry and embittered Romulan from the future enacts revenge on Spock and his Vulcan race for not being able to save his planet Romulus. With his massive ship he drills a hole into the core of planet Vulcan and inserts ‘red matter’ into the core. This creates a black hole that absorbs the planet committing genocide upon the 6 billion inhabitant Vulcan race (apart from Spock, his father and a few ‘elders’). This grim aspect of the plot takes the normally light-hearted Star Trek to a whole new level of ‘shit just got serious’ seriousness. However, something about these Vulcans just don't add up. The Planet Vulcan Spock and the Vulcan race are supposed to be one of the most intelligent race of beings in the galaxy. One of their biggest traits is to maintain logic over emotion at all times. They store and process information at a volume and speed exponentially greater than humans, they are adept at learning and transmitting knowledge and their analytical skills and foresight would make living Chess legend Magnus Carlsen look like a baboon playing with his toy. Yet look at where they live. This shithole is planet Vulcan. As you can see it is a wasteland full of rocks and sand. As brilliant as these Vulcans are, their architecture looks like a bombed out Cairo at best. Vulcans are humanoid. They need food, water and sex to procreate. They admire beauty, they fall in love and they have something of a sense of humour. Their planet looks to be 20% water within a huge, dry continent devoid of vegetation of any sort. How did their population manage to reach six billion living on a hot, arid and infertile planet? Why did they never decided to colonize a more agreeable and unoccupied planet? I'm pretty sure the Federation would allow it. If they are so advanced in technology why can't they properly develop their planet and find means of increasing and distributing their water supply or getting some trees to grow? Are the Vulcan's really that smart? The Vulcans have the ability to create black holes at an instant yet they have zero defense against Romulan ships blasting holes deep into the core of their planet. They have no planetary shield, no defense satellite, no space army, they don't even have ships to escort their people off the planet. They depend entirely on Starfleet to repel the enemy and evacuate the people. Yet we're supposed to believe them to be creatures of the highest logic. The Vulcans have sent a distress call to Starfleet about their planet being attacked. I'm guessing the distress call was a bit like this: ‘Hey bros send help. Some idiot is drilling a hole into our crappy planet. It's making a lot of noise and really annoying.’ ‘Hey sorry. Forgot to warn you that they have a massive ship, 50 times bigger than the biggest Starfleet warship and using technology and weaponry that is so powerful that it most likely comes from the future. ‘Hope you sent warships and the Starfleet army and not just your student trainees and scout ships…..you did! Crap.’ ‘We’ll just go offer our prayers to our giant stone idols in our primitive church cave where you can't get a signal to beam us to safety.’ ‘If anything just send Spock to come get us.’ That aspect of the film is so utterly ludicrous that it takes me out of the movie a tad bit. Great movie nonetheless. This is the only plot hole that comes to mind when I think about this movie but I have seen worse.Take the 2007 film ‘I Am Legend‘ starring Will Smith. I love this movie to bits and I’m not ashamed to admit that the 2007 Robert Neville character is the best role that Will Smith has ever played. The basic premise of the movie is simple and well done. A New York City scientist (Will Smith) is the only human survivor of a man-made plague that wipes out the entire human race. The plague converts humans into a vampire-like state where they are extremely sensitive to the sun (the ‘Darkseekers’). Neville lives a solitary life in a desolated New York City where he spends his days trying to find a cure for the plague and his nights barricaded in his house trying to evade the Darkseekers’ attempt to kill him. The main plot hole arises when he finally finds the cure, or at least, the means of creating the cure. He does this by experimenting on one of the Darkseekers that he captured in his house. The Darkseeker, a female one, becomes the key to the creation of the cure. Neville creates an antidote serum and administers it to her. The serum works after a few tries. Neville realizes that the cure can be injected into living Darkseekers. The Darkseekers don't like this very much and constantly attack Neville in an effort to rescue the captured female Darkseeker. They break into his house and take the infected female captive so they can get her out to safety. Neville is able to defeat the Darkseekers in a hail of gunfire and then sacrifices himself in order to destroy as many Darkseekers as he can. Neville creates a cure and then sacrifices himself to save humanity. Sounds great right?

What actors were supposed to be the next best thing in Hollywood but never made it? Hollywood is littered with the ghosts of actors who were touted as the next big thing, only to fade into relative obscurity. The film industry, much like any high-stakes game, is a fickle mistress. Some actors, blessed with talent, charisma, and the right connections, ascend to the A-list with seemingly effortless grace. Others, despite possessing all the necessary ingredients for success, find their careers stalling, burdened by missteps, poor choices, or simply, bad luck. The "next big thing" label is often bestowed upon rising stars based on a potent cocktail of box office potential, critical acclaim, and studio hype. However, what audiences often fail to consider is the unpredictable nature of fame itself. One wrong role, a string of flops, or a change in personal circumstances can derail even the most promising careers. Take for instance, Taylor Kitsch. This Canadian actor, brimming with boyish charm, was poised for superstardom. He was cast in a string of high-profile projects, like "Friday Night Lights," "X-Men Origins: Wolverine," and "John Carter." He had the looks, the acting chops, and a fanbase eager to see him reach the heights. Yet, despite the hype and promise, Kitsch never quite broke through. Each film he starred in seemed to underperform, which led to him being branded as a financial risk. Now, he works primarily on TV and smaller film projects.Another name that immediately springs to mind is Sam Worthington. After starring in the highest grossing movie of all time "Avatar" and the critically acclaimed "Clash of the Titans," many expected his trajectory to follow that of a typical action hero. Yet, this never actually happened. He featured in a few more action films, none of which managed to impress. Worthington, like Kitsch, faded from the limelight, a victim of bad luck and poor choices. Some actors never get the right role to elevate them to the stratosphere, and for them, that is that. Hollywood is certainly a cutthroat business.

What do fast food employees think of customers who come in frequently, say, multiple times a week or even daily? As someone who has eaten fast food, I can certainly give you some insights. My friend worked at a popular fried chicken chain in the capital, so his daily interactions with customers provided an interesting window. Essentially, a fast food employee quickly categorizes their customers. Regulars are, of course, are known figures in the restaurant. You’ll see them often. They are familiar, they are expected. Some are appreciated, some are not. They may have a specific order. Some customers are genuinely friendly and pleasant, and are always welcomed back and remembered fondly by the employees. These are the customers who brighten up their day and make the job less tedious. They are considered a delight.But then again, some regulars are not seen in the same light. They are often the ones who are demanding, entitled, or rude. Maybe they are always complaining about something, or are overly particular, or make excessive requests. Or perhaps they are unkempt or smell a bit unpleasant, and are always the same. Perhaps they seem to live there. These customers are less welcomed as they often make the work environment more difficult and are usually the ones who would make the employees more annoyed and frustrated. They are the ones who create the headaches.Most fast food employees are just trying to get through their shift. Being at the mercy of public interactions, they have very little control over the customer encounters, so having regular, problematic customers can add an extra layer of stress. This is particularly evident during peak hours when efficiency is paramount. These are the customers who add the extra pressure.

What is legal but ethically wrong? It's a thorny question, right? Things that are permissible under the law but still manage to feel dirty - like a bad handshake that leaves a residue of unspoken tension. I always find myself drawn to these gray areas, more so than the clear cut cases of right and wrong. Perhaps it is the Agribusiness Management and IT background in me that makes me want to analyze everything.You see, I grew up in a predominantly English-speaking context, though not a native one. We in Trinidad and Tobago are known for our unique perspective, a blend of Caribbean charm and a healthy dose of skepticism. We Trinis are not easily fazed, and that is a good base when navigating the ethical landscape.There's a certain level of cultural relativism in the Caribbean, a recognition that what is accepted in one society might be frowned upon in another. It's a good lesson in humility, and reminds me of the importance of empathy. These very grey areas are the things that I find interesting. Something in my childhood of philosophy, writing, and media analysis keeps me on the path of learning and better understanding. I believe that's what makes us human.

Which extremely surreal film would you consider to be worth watching? In my opinion, David Lynch’s Mulholland Drive is the quintessential surrealist film, a cinematic enigma that burrows deep into the subconscious. The movie is a labyrinth of dreams, shadows, and fragmented realities, where nothing is quite as it seems and the viewer is perpetually left grasping at elusive clues. The narrative, if one can even call it that, unfolds like a series of half-remembered events, a tapestry woven with vivid imagery and a haunting score. I would suggest watching it, multiple times if possible, as each viewing unveils new layers and interpretations. It's a journey best undertaken with an open mind, ready to embrace the unsettling and the unexplained. The film’s genius lies in its ability to subvert expectations and defy easy categorization. Unlike many surrealist films that prioritize shock value over substance, Mulholland Drive has an emotional core that resonates long after the credits roll. The performances are uniformly excellent, with Naomi Watts delivering a career-defining performance. The film’s ambiguity keeps the plot fresh, inviting us to construct our own meaning, thereby making us active participants in the storytelling process; something that is rarely achieved in movies. The tone is both alluring and disquieting, a blend of glamour and dread that keeps you on edge. It’s a film that refuses to be understood, challenging viewers to delve into its mysteries and grapple with its ambiguities. For all of its complexity, the film is beautifully shot, with a careful attention to detail that elevates its surreal qualities.

Without saying their name, who is your favorite fictional character? This is difficult because I have numerous favorite fictional characters. As an avid consumer of books, comics, movies and television shows over the years, I have, at any given time, several fictional characters who I admire, emulate and try to analyze. However, if I had to choose one, it would be *him.* He's a bit of an anti-hero, a man of the cloth but not quite. He always does the right thing, no matter the consequence. He's a fighter, a bit of a brute, but he isn't evil. He can be reckless but he's always clever. He cares deeply about the ones he loves even when he doesn't show it. He's witty and sarcastic yet compassionate. He operates in a world of grey where good and evil are never black and white. He is capable of profound introspection which contradicts the very world he moves in. He has flaws; huge flaws, which on occasion clouds his judgement, yet he doesn’t let these failures define him, he learns from them instead. He’s a leader, a pragmatist, a man of action. He makes mistakes. Sometimes he suffers terribly. He is *the complete* package, everything I would love to be. He’s flawed, because he isn't perfect. He's human, because he’s not a god. He's a character I'm constantly reevaluating, often changing my mind on his worth, his actions and his ultimate motives, but still there’s never been a time I have not considered him the ideal man. A man of action, conviction, who would gladly sacrifice his very existence for the greater good. That is why, to this day, he is my favorite character.

Would Hollywood actor Brad Pitt have made it in old or classic Hollywood back in the day? I'd wager he would have, absolutely. To even begin to address this question, we must first dissect what constitutes ‘old’ or ‘classic’ Hollywood. It was an era unlike any other in film history, a period defined by many unique characteristics. Think of the unparalleled studio system, where actors and actresses were molded and marketed by powerful studios. The studio bosses had near-total control. Image, public perception, and the overall persona were carefully curated. The stars were larger than life, and their private lives were often as carefully managed as their on-screen roles. Then there was the advent of technology. We're talking about the transition from silent films to talkies, the rise of Technicolor, and the evolution of filmmaking techniques. The stars had to be charismatic as their voices were now vital to the performance. Could Brad Pitt conceivably adapt with the times? Without question.He possesses an undeniable level of charisma and a screen presence that has captivated audiences for decades. He has proven himself to be more than merely a pretty face. What was the first thing you saw, heard or discovered that made you feel old? The first thing that truly made me feel old? It wasn't a physical ache, a gray hair, or a sudden fondness for prune juice, though those things have definitely crept in. No, it wasn't something I saw, heard, or even discovered, in the traditional sense. It was the realization that the music I grew up with – the stuff that defined my teenage years, the soundtrack to my first loves and heartbreaks, the very pulse of a generation – was now considered "classic rock." Yup, classic rock. As if it was some ancient artifact, a relic of a bygone era. I remember the exact moment. I was in a car, minding my own business, when a song by Nirvana (yes, Nirvana!) came on the radio. The local station, usually playing the latest pop hits, had started a "Classic Rock" segment, and there it was, blaring from the speakers. My initial reaction was confusion. *Nirvana?* Classic? My brain refused to compute. It was like someone had told me that my favorite pair of worn-out jeans were now museum pieces. Then, the reality hit me. Those songs, which were the soundtrack of my angst-ridden youth, were now being played for a new generation, a generation that probably thought Kurt Cobain was some historical figure. Suddenly, I felt a pang of...well, not nostalgia, but a strange, creeping sense of detachment. I was no longer part of the "now," I was a spectator, gazing upon a past that was fast becoming history. It wasn't a massive epiphany, but a quiet surrender to the slow, inevitable march of time. And that, my friends, was when I first felt truly, undeniably, old.
